whatItDoes: Projects your retirement balance by compounding current savings together with monthly contributions over your chosen number of years to retirement. Shows the projected balance, your total contributions, and the growth earned so you can see the contribution-vs-return split clearly.
whyItExists: The biggest influence on retirement readiness is time in the market plus consistent saving. Showing the projected balance and the contribution-growth split makes it easy to see how much your money does for you over decades.
whoShouldUse: Anyone building a retirement nest egg — salaried employees with 401(k)s or IRAs, self-employed savers, and early-career workers — who wants a realistic projection of how monthly contributions and returns interact.
useCases: Project a 401(k) or IRA balance at retirement
See the impact of raising monthly contributions
Estimate the total you'll actually contribute
Compare starting now vs. delaying by a few years
Check whether employer matching materially changes the projection
instructions: Enter your current retirement savings balance
Enter your monthly contribution amount (include employer match)
Enter an expected annual return as a percent
Read the projected balance, total contributions, and growth
Adjust inputs to test scenarios like higher contributions or later retirement
examples: $0 saved, $500/month, 7% for 40 years → ≈ $1.31M, of which only $240,000 is your own money
bestPractices: Use a conservative return you're comfortable assuming (6-8% is common)
Re-run as your income and contributions grow
Include employer matching if you have it — it's free money
Check the growth vs. contributions split to see compounding's effect
Start now — delaying even 5 years significantly cuts the end balance
commonMistakes: Starting contributions at the top of your budget with no buffer
Ignoring taxes and inflation in the real value
Assuming the same contribution rate will last the whole working life
Forgetting to re-check the projection after a job change or income raise
faq: Does this include taxes and inflation? — No, it is a nominal pre-tax projection.
What return should I use? — A common assumption is 6-8%, but use your own planning number.
Is employer matching included? — Only if you add it to the monthly contribution.
Is my data shared? — No, everything runs locally in your browser.
How much should I save for retirement? — A common rule of thumb is 15% of gross income, but the right number depends on your goals and timeline.
Is it better to save more or start earlier? — Both matter, but time is the strongest lever because of compounding.
